El infinito en un junco: Many people recommended it, and Prophecy calls it a marvel. I loved Prophecy, so I believed it. So far it's how easily she tells it, turning history into a story you want to follow. I'm still at the beginning.
Good Strategy Bad Strategy: A way of thinking about strategy that pulls me out of the lazy habit of avoiding the hardest questions in building a product. I come back to it often when I'm thinking at a strategic level. Useful for everyone, and especially for people in product, to frame our plans well.
Music Law in the Digital Age: A clear map of digital music licensing, behind all my licensing work. I use it all the time, for reviewing contracts and for the data tools I build. For anyone building a digital product that music licensing runs through.
Inspired: A good reminder that gets me excited about discovery again. For every product manager, especially those who come from other fields. It gives us a shared language and shared ways of framing a conversation.
Never Split the Difference: Its ways of thinking about concessions, a method for structuring difficult conversations, and a mental model that makes any negotiation more interesting and cooperative. I use it all the time, especially in music licensing. For anyone who wants better mental models for reaching an agreement.
Prophecy: Her reflections on the algorithms that shape today's world, and the questions to ask when predictions, projections and statistical conclusions are everywhere. It stays with me constantly, especially when I want to remember how to question a statistical result. For everyone, really.
La perra: The way she tells it, and how completely she becomes a character. I read it one humid summer, and it took me right into the Pacific coast of the Chocó. For anyone who wants a book to absorb them, body and mind.
Los abismos: The heat of Cali and its reflections on imperfect mothers. I read it travelling around Colombia. For anyone who wants to discover more of the wonderful Colombian women writers we're lucky to have.
Lo que no tiene nombre: The depth, and at the same time the calm, of Piedad's reflections on something so hard. I read it in one sitting on a Sunday afternoon. Time went by softly and it was over before I knew it. For anyone going through a hard grief.
Donde cantan las ballenas: Its ending still shakes me. Magical realism, seen through the eyes of a little girl. It took me years, because I had to wait until I was ready to finish it. For anyone in love with the magical realism that is so much our continent's own.
Mujeres que corren con los lobos: Its deep connection with the feminine symbols in our psyche. It helped me get back on my feet at a very hard time. For all women. It's our bible.
La clase de griego: The beauty of its synaesthetic descriptions, and above all his letters, which are so lovely. I read it in a couple of days and didn't want to stop. For anyone who enjoys novels that care less about the plot than about the atmosphere around it.
La vegetariana: Its deep and careful reflection on femininity and the body in society. I read it over a couple of nights. For anyone asking themselves what the self is, and what freedom is.
La ridícula idea de no volver a verte: How a biography of Marie Curie could make me cry, I still don't know. Rosa Montero's voice is incredible. I read it slowly over a couple of weeks and didn't want it to end. For anyone looking to give their grief a voice.
